findings.title: Blueprint users lose data wires and branch semantics on paste — clipboard mapper discards data edges and pin identities
findings.surface: Event Graph > Copy for Unreal; plugin Blueprints/*_EventGraph.txt
findings.observed: Files, media and generated artifacts: source predicts that a supported stored graph with a variable feeding a branch condition loses that data wire entirely. Branch outputs are assigned then/else solely by edge iteration order, with no stored pin identity to determine whether the first destination belongs to True or False. Developers cannot obtain the promised working nodes and wires; behavior can be reversed or disconnected, requiring manual graph reconstruction. No Unreal paste was executed.
findings.evidence: server.py:137-140 NodeGraphEdge stores only from_node/to_node/kind, not source/destination pin names. unrealExtras.js:59 filters edges to '(e.kind || "exec") === "exec"'; :63-64 chooses an output by edge iteration order rather than node.outputs or edge source identity; :62 only connects to 'execute'; :81 emits every generated pin with PinCategory="exec". Workspace.jsx:575-579 copies this output and zipExport.js:184 writes it to the plugin.
findings.expected: request: "pasting into a Blueprint editor (Ctrl+V) creates the real nodes and wires" and "branches, variables (get/set), sequence and delays"; R-289/R-290 require preserving node and pin connections. Data edges, value pin types and branch output identities must survive export independently of array ordering.
reproduction_steps: Open a system whose graph includes a variable-get node feeding a Branch via a data edge.
Press Copy for Unreal, or export its plugin and inspect the Blueprint paste file.
The produced text contains no value/Condition connection.
For a branching graph, compare its desired output labels to export: edges are assigned then and else by list position, not their actual output pin.

findings.title: Retrying a failed test fix can patch the component instead — Retry drops the tests target
findings.surface: Tests > Fix these > error > Try again
findings.observed: Business logic and calculations: if a test patch times out or cannot match, Try again sends the same test issues against the main component implementation, presents a main-code diff, and Accept changes the component, not the test. The automatic recovery route can alter valid production code and never repairs the test. Developers can cancel/reopen the original test Fix as a workaround, but the erroneous accepted output can materially change the system.
findings.evidence: Workspace.jsx:964 initially calls runFix(l,null,"tests"); :619 defaults target to "code"; :624 chooses test vs component source from that target. Retry at :1175 calls runFix(fix.list,fix.thenExport) without target. :653-658 then applies both returned files to main C++, while the test branch :641-651 is bypassed.
findings.expected: R-294: tests "can be fixed the same way"; checklist, Business logic and calculations: "retry ... reaches valid work for the same operation." A test-fix retry must keep the test source and target, never switch to production implementation.
reproduction_steps: Open Tests with a reported missing include.
Press Fix and encounter a timeout or patch_failed response.
Press Try again.
Inspect the second request/review: its .cpp is now the component implementation.
Accept: main C++ changes while the test file is unchanged.

findings.title: Undoing a deletion can insert code into the wrong function or duplicate it — empty added hunks match any old line number
findings.surface: History > past deletion fix > Undo this fix
findings.observed: Business logic and calculations: undoing a fix that only deleted lines after another change inserts lines above that gap restores the removed code at the old numeric position, potentially inside another function/declaration. Repeated Undo also inserts the deleted block repeatedly because the empty added sequence always matches. This produces materially incorrect C++ while reporting success; only manual review or a whole-version restore recovers it.
findings.evidence: fixLog.js:35 defines at(i) using h.added.every(...); for a deletion h.added is [], so this is always true. :36-37 accepts the original h.start unconditionally for empty added, then :43 inserts h.removed there. No surrounding context is stored in hunk(:13) or verified.
findings.expected: R-333/request: undo "just that fix", "even if the code above has shifted"; "If the lines changed since ... nothing changes". For a deletion, identify the original gap from anchored context or refuse ambiguity, never insert at an unrelated stale line.
reproduction_steps: Accept/save a fix deleting a block of code at line 20.
Apply another fix inserting five lines above line 20, leaving the deletion's neighborhood otherwise untouched.
In History choose the deletion fix > Undo this fix.
The removed block is inserted at line 20 rather than the shifted location at line 25; invoking Undo again inserts it again.

findings.title: Long fixes cannot be accurately viewed or undone and can damage code — history silently truncates each file's change span to 400 lines
findings.surface: Fix History for long C++ files
findings.observed: Files, media and generated artifacts: for supported imported/long code with two changes more than 400 lines apart, history omits the second change. If the first change adds a line, Undo replaces 400 added lines with 400 removed lines whose endpoints differ, drops an unchanged boundary line, and leaves the later change applied. It reports success despite corrupting source and not undoing that fix. The 40k/60k API code bounds permit this workload.
findings.evidence: fixLog.js:4-13 combines all changes in a file into one span and independently slices removed and added to MAX=400; makeFixEntry :22 stores these truncated spans, FixDetailModal.jsx:93-95 displays them, and undoFixEntry :43 replaces only the truncated added span with truncated removed.
findings.expected: request/R-331/R-333: "Show every accepted fix ... before/after again" and "undo just that fix". Retain the complete changed content or reject a history entry too large to undo safely; do not silently truncate an operation.
reproduction_steps: Import a system whose .cpp exceeds 450 short lines.
Accept one fix adding an include near the top and changing another line beyond line 450.
Save and View the fix: the latter edit is missing.
Undo this fix: only the truncated prefix span is replaced, not the whole accepted operation.

findings.title: A downgraded teammate can retain Editor access — concurrent invites create duplicate memberships and role changes update only the first
findings.surface: Team/project Invite and role downgrade endpoints
findings.observed: Auth, sessions and access control: two owner tabs inviting the same new email concurrently can both pass the absence check, store duplicate entries and send different tokens. If an unverified password-account user accepts the second Editor entry, changing their role to Viewer updates only the first entry; the second user_id-bound Editor continues authorizing writes. The owner is unable to revoke edit authority with the role control despite a successful downgrade response. Removing the member entirely can recover safely but is not the requested Viewer access.
findings.evidence: teams.py:125 reads members then :131 unconditionally $pushes a new member when absent; :139 role changes use positional members.$ (first match). projects.py:414-418 and :427 have the same read-check-push/first-update pattern. No uniqueness/atomic email exclusion exists. teams.py:22-28 selects the member matching user_id, and projects.py:35-37 likewise grants its role.
findings.expected: R-336: downgrade "takes effect on that member's next request"; checklist, Data, persistence and APIs: "store-enforced uniqueness" and "walk plausible interleavings". One invitation/membership per normalized address must be enforced atomically; changing a person's role must update their effective membership.
reproduction_steps: As team/project owner use two tabs to invite the same previously absent email as Editor concurrently.
Have that email's password account accept the link from the second stored invitation.
Change the member to Viewer.
That account's next save still derives Editor from its unchanged user_id-bound entry.

findings.title: Reset recipients can be sent to a foreign site with their token — email URLs trust an unvalidated request host
findings.surface: POST /api/auth/forgot-password; invite email URL construction
findings.observed: Auth, sessions and access control: if the ingress preserves a caller-supplied forwarded-host header (or permits arbitrary Host), an unauthenticated forgot-password caller can make the real reset email direct the recipient's single-use token to a different HTTPS site. A recipient following that authentic-looking email exposes the token there, allowing account takeover and access to their projects. The source lacks host enforcement; whether the deployed proxy overwrites those headers is not available, so reach is conditional on that stated ingress behavior, not runtime-tested.
findings.evidence: emailer.app_url(:95) derives the trusted email link host directly from x-forwarded-host or host, with no configured-origin comparison. auth.py:279 embeds that URL plus the reset token in the actual email sent at :280. _assert_safe_email(:79-83) permits any ordinary HTTPS hostname. server.py:740-751 installs no host-validation middleware.
findings.expected: R-284/request: reset link "opens the app's reset page directly"; checklist, Auth, sessions and access control: server-derived authority stays authoritative; checklist, Third-party integrations: requests must "leak nothing." Use a trusted configured app origin or an explicitly trusted/validated proxy host for sensitive links.
reproduction_steps: On a deployment that forwards caller-supplied forwarded-host values, request a password reset for an existing account while supplying a different HTTPS hostname via that header.
Inspect the app_url/template path: the emailed reset link uses that hostname, not the app origin.
If the recipient follows it, the token is delivered to the other site's reset URL.

findings.title: A substituted Google callback can sign a visitor into someone else's workspace — the new pending flag is not bound to the OAuth transaction
findings.surface: Continue with Google; AuthCallback; POST /api/auth/google
findings.observed: Auth, sessions and access control: source predicts login CSRF if a visitor has started (or abandoned) Google sign-in in that tab and then follows a substituted callback carrying another person's valid session id. The boolean admits it without tying it to the initiated sign-in; the server has no corresponding check. The victim can unknowingly generate and save private game-system code in that other account, where its owner can read it. This is conditional on delivering a valid substituted callback while the flag exists; no exploit or provider transaction was executed.
findings.evidence: Login.jsx:36 writes the constant '1' to sessionStorage and :39 redirects without any app-generated state; AuthPages.jsx:20 only tests that the flag exists and :26 posts the supplied session_id. auth.py:165 accepts only body and response (no browser-bound request/state), :167 retrieves any supplied valid provider session and :189-193 installs it as this browser's session. Projects are saved under the resulting user_id (projects.py:136).
findings.expected: checklist, Auth, sessions and access control: OAuth callbacks 'validate issued state' and 'server-derived authority stays authoritative'. The builder's new browser-started-sign-in safeguard must bind the returned provider session to the actual transaction, not just to any prior click in that tab.
reproduction_steps: In a visitor tab, start Continue with Google, then abandon that sign-in without completing it.
Return in the same tab using a callback link associated with a different valid provider session.
Source predicts that AuthCallback accepts the pending flag and the backend installs the unrelated account session.
A project saved afterwards belongs to that unrelated account.

findings.title: Signing out after access-token expiry leaves the refresh session valid — revocation only resolves an unexpired access identity
findings.surface: Account menu > Sign out; POST /api/auth/logout; POST /api/auth/refresh
findings.observed: Auth, sessions and access control: for an email/password user who leaves the workspace idle beyond the 15-minute access lifetime and signs out before another API request refreshes it, logout resolves no user and does not revoke the still-live seven-day refresh token. A retained/copied refresh credential can obtain new access after the user signed out, allowing continued reading and changing private projects. Source proves the expired-access condition bypasses revocation; it does not assert that a credential has actually been stolen.
findings.evidence: auth.py:76-87 optional_user checks access JWTs, Google sessions and bearer tokens, never refresh_token; :58-60 rejects expired access JWTs. logout at :220-221 increments token_version only when optional_user succeeds, otherwise just deletes browser cookies. refresh at :204-212 accepts an existing refresh token with unchanged token_version.
findings.expected: checklist, Auth, sessions and access control: 'Sign-out ... ends a server-held session' and 'next-request rejection of revoked ... sessions'. The requested sign-out must revoke the refresh authority even when its short-lived access token has expired.
reproduction_steps: Sign in using email/password.
Let the access token expire (15 minutes) without making a protected request; the refresh credential remains valid.
Choose Sign out.
A caller retaining that refresh credential can still call /api/auth/refresh and obtain access because token_version was never incremented.

findings.title: Phone users cannot reliably reach AI-key setup or the result — the new flow remains inside a clipped fixed-width desktop workspace

The two non-shrinking sidebars alone require 320+340=660px before any central workspace width; the non-wrapping header places the new AI-key button after several actions, outside the clipped viewport. A phone user has no responsive menu or horizontal document scroll to reach the key setup and central result normally. This blocks the essential first-key/synthesis workflow for that cohort; the modal's own max-width is responsive if opened, but does not fix its inaccessible entry point. No browser layout measurement was performed.
findings.evidence: Workspace.jsx:444 uses a single non-wrapping header with brand, JSON actions, Save, AI-key and account controls; :488 fixes the left sidebar at 320px shrink-0 and :678 fixes the right sidebar at 340px shrink-0. App.css:1 sets width:100vw and overflow:hidden; index.css:57-59 also prevents document scrolling. There is no responsive replacement for these header/sidebar elements.

The new key settings entry point and synthesis result must remain reachable on the supported narrow screen.

Try to reach Add AI key in the top bar and then view a synthesis result.
The fixed-width, non-wrapping desktop layout exceeds the viewport while the app/document hide overflow; no small-screen navigation is supplied.

findings.title: A late save response can cause the next save to overwrite the wrong project — metadata is replaced without checking the active project
findings.surface: Save project while opening another project
findings.observed: UI state, navigation and interaction: start saving A, open B before the response, then receive A's save response. The header/role/version become A while the visible result and inputs remain B. A subsequent Save writes B's system into A using A's fresh version, with no conflict warning. This can overwrite another project's valid work with unrelated code under an apparently normal save. Version history may retain the old output, but it does not prevent the wrong-target save and there is no direct restore control. Source predicts consequential cross-project corruption for this reachable slow-save timing.
findings.evidence: Workspace.jsx:298-300 starts a save for the project in the handler closure; :302 unconditionally sets returned metadata as current. ProjectsPanel.jsx:90 leaves project-open buttons enabled while saving; openProject at Workspace.jsx:338-339 changes both metadata and result. splitResult at :289 then reads whichever result is currently shown and the next save at :299 uses whichever metadata the late save installed.
findings.expected: checklist, UI state, navigation and interaction: 'stale work must respect later decisions'; checklist, Data, persistence and APIs: preserve object 'identity ... including late client responses'. A response for project A must not relabel project B's open output or redirect its next save to A.
reproduction_steps: Open editable project A and click Save.
Before that request returns, click Open on project B in Projects.
Let A's save finish: A's name reappears while B's system remains displayed.
Click Save: the handler sends B's system to A's project URL.

findings.title: Anyone signed in with an invite link can take the invited teammate's access — acceptance never checks the invited email or consumes the token
findings.surface: /invite/:token; POST /api/invites/{token}/accept
findings.observed: Auth, sessions and access control: source predicts a signed-in recipient of a forwarded or leaked invite link can bind it to a different email, read the team's system and files, and, for an Editor invite, overwrite work. Reusing the link reassigns user_id again, potentially displacing the intended teammate. No owner approval is required; owner removal of the member is the available recovery.
findings.evidence: backend/projects.py:226 looks up only members.invite_token; :229-230 sets members.$.user_id to the caller without comparing members.email or marking the invite used. role_for at :33-35 grants the bound user that member's role. frontend/src/pages/AuthPages.jsx:72-75 automatically accepts the token.
findings.expected: R-076: "is refused when the caller's email differs from the invited address" and "only once"; request: "An invite is sent to an email address." Acceptance must bind only that address and must not let another account replay it.
reproduction_steps: As owner, invite teammate A as Editor and copy the invite link.
Sign in with a different email B and open that link.
The code accepts B and opens the project with Editor access.
Open the same link as another signed-in account; the membership is rebound again.

findings.title: Two editors can silently overwrite each other's saves — version check is separate from the unconditional update
findings.surface: Save; PUT /api/projects/{id}
findings.observed: Data, persistence and APIs: source predicts that two editors saving from version 1 concurrently can both pass the read-time check before either update. Both writes then succeed (versions 2 and 3), with the latter replacing the former system and inputs, and neither editor receives an overwrite warning. Consequential generated team work is lost without history (Phase 2 is not implemented).
findings.evidence: backend/projects.py:163-168 reads and compares the version, then :169-172 find_one_and_update filters only project_id and increments version. frontend/src/pages/Workspace.jsx:273 sends base_version and :281 shows the warning only on 409.
findings.expected: R-068: "you are warned before overwriting"; R-069: an older base_version "returns 409 ... and writes nothing"; checklist, Data, persistence and APIs: "conditional/atomic operations" must protect concurrent commit points. Exactly one version-1 save may commit without a warning.
reproduction_steps: Owner and Editor open the same version of a project.
Make different changes in each workspace.
Press Save in both while the requests overlap so both load the old version before either update.
Both return success; reopen and observe that only the later system remains, without a conflict dialog.

findings.title: Removed teammates can still fetch their uploaded project files — uploader bypass skips current project permissions
findings.surface: GET /api/files/{file_id}; DELETE /api/files/{file_id}; generation references
findings.observed: Auth, sessions and access control: source predicts a removed Editor retains authenticated download access to every project file they uploaded even after membership removal or project deletion, and retains delete/use-in-generation access to their references after demotion to Viewer. This defeats the team's revocation boundary; the owner cannot revoke this file access through Share or project deletion.
findings.evidence: backend/projects.py:311-312 returns any file directly to its uploader for a viewer/read check, before :314 load_project. For reference files it also returns directly for editor/delete checks. :187-189 deleting a project only marks the project deleted and never marks files deleted. :341-349 loads references using this same bypass.
findings.expected: Request: "Members can upload, download and delete files, according to their role"; R-065: deletion "removes the project and its files"; checklist, Auth, sessions and access control: "Follow ... membership removal ... through every supported access path." Project-linked files must always enforce the current project role and live-project state.
reproduction_steps: As Editor upload a project file and attach a reference; retain their file ids.
As owner remove this Editor in Share (or delete the project).
As the former Editor request download of the uploaded file by its existing file id.
The uploader shortcut still serves it; a reference can also still be deleted or used in generation.

findings.title: Opening another project during synthesis can save the first project's output over it — late completion is not tied to its project
findings.surface: Synthesize → Projects → open → Save
findings.observed: UI state, navigation and interaction: source predicts a user generating A can open B during the 40–90 second job; A's delayed result then replaces B's displayed system while B's name, role and version stay selected. Pressing Save writes A's code and inputs over B without a conflict because B's version is current. There is no version history to recover B's overwritten system. The running task needs an operation/project identity guard or navigation protection.
findings.evidence: Workspace.jsx:187 awaits generation then :188-191 unconditionally replaces result using the original closure. :305-311 can independently replace project and result while the await runs. ProjectsPanel.jsx:90 open buttons remain enabled while busy (only Stack at :76 uses busy). Workspace.jsx:273 subsequently saves the displayed result to the currently selected project's id.
findings.expected: Request: projects hold their own "latest generated system" and inputs; checklist, Business logic and calculations: "stale work must respect later decisions"; checklist, UI state, navigation and interaction: "including late completion after cancel" and context restoration must preserve valid work.
reproduction_steps: Open A and start a regeneration.
Before it finishes, click B's Open row in Projects.
Wait for A's generation to finish; the header still names B but result/context come from A.
Press Save, then reopen B; its previous output has been replaced by A's generation.

findings.title: A pre-registered password retains access to the real Google user's projects — account linking trusts an unverified existing email
findings.surface: Email registration → Google account linking → email sign-in
findings.observed: Auth, sessions and access control: source predicts someone who pre-registers a teammate's email can keep their chosen password after the real teammate signs in with Google. The real teammate sees a successful Google session and creates private projects in the same user_id; the earlier registrant can log in by password to read or modify those projects and files. No victim password or Google credentials are required for the pre-registration. The victim would need owner-assisted reset to regain sole access.
findings.evidence: auth.py:127-134 permits registering an unverified email with a password. :168-171 merges a subsequent Google sign-in into that row and sets email_verified True, without removing or re-proving its existing password. :147-156 continues accepting that password. Project ownership is keyed by user_id (projects.py:31).
findings.expected: R-055: "same email address ... one account" must preserve secure identity; checklist, Auth, sessions and access control: "Establish the actual principals and trust model" and "OAuth ... link/create once". Linking a provider-verified email must not leave an unrelated unverified registrant with ongoing access.
reproduction_steps: Register an email/password account using another person's email (without email verification).
Have the actual email owner sign in through Google with that address and save a private project.
Sign in with the password chosen during pre-registration.
That session has the same user_id and can access the real owner's newly saved work.

findings.title: Signing out does not revoke email sessions — access and refresh JWTs have no server-side session or revocation check
findings.surface: Sign out; POST /api/auth/logout and /refresh; authenticated APIs
findings.observed: Auth, sessions and access control: source predicts a retained email access token can continue reading and writing private projects for its remaining 15 minutes after Sign out; a retained refresh credential can mint further access for seven days. Clearing the UI cookies does not invalidate a captured session. Signing out therefore cannot terminate a compromised/shared email session; Google sessions do have a database deletion path.
findings.evidence: auth.py:32 JWT payload has sub/type/exp but no session identity; :55-62 validates signature and user existence only. Logout :207-210 deletes only Google session rows and client cookies. Refresh :196-201 accepts the previous signed refresh token without a revoked-session lookup.
findings.expected: Request: "sign-out"; checklist, Auth, sessions and access control: "next-request rejection of revoked/deleted sessions" and "Sign-out ... ends a server-held session." A signed-out email session must not remain usable with its old credentials.
reproduction_steps: Sign in with email/password and retain that session's credentials in an authorized API client.
Use Account menu → Sign out.
Reuse the old access credential for GET /api/projects; it remains accepted until expiry.
Reuse the old refresh credential for POST /api/auth/refresh; it can still renew access.

findings.title: Unsolicited Google callbacks can log a visitor into another account — callback exchange lacks browser-bound state validation
findings.surface: Google sign-in callback
findings.observed: Auth, sessions and access control: source predicts an unsolicited callback URL containing a valid broker session identifier for a different account is exchanged and sets that account's session cookie, without proof that this browser initiated that login. A signed-out visitor can be logged into another person's account and unknowingly save private UE5 work there. Broker-side validity proves the identifier's identity, not this browser's intent; actual broker issuance behavior was not executed.
findings.evidence: Login.jsx:35-38 starts broker auth with redirect only, with no app nonce. App.js:21 accepts any session_id fragment. AuthPages.jsx:18-19 exchanges it immediately. auth.py:161-163 receives only session_id and verifies it with the provider but never binds it to a browser-initiated state.
findings.expected: R-054: "checks the OAuth state value issued at sign-in start ... a callback whose state value does not match is refused"; checklist, Auth, sessions and access control: "validate issued state." An uninitiated callback must not change the browser's signed-in identity.
reproduction_steps: Obtain a valid broker callback identifier for account A in a controlled authentication flow.
In a different signed-out browser that never started Google login, open the app callback location carrying that identifier.
The frontend posts it and the backend sets account A's cookie without checking browser-bound state.
Saving work would then store it under A.

findings.title: Regeneration and stacking cannot preserve existing implementation — both discard source, pseudocode, graph and most code before calling Claude
findings.surface: Regenerate and Stack Systems model context
findings.observed: AI and model features: source proves custom behavior contained only in the previous .cpp, pseudocode, setup, graph or the omitted header tail is never sent on regeneration or stacking. For example, a saved damage system with a bespoke combo-reset rule only in its .cpp cannot have that rule preserved from the provided context when the user only changes Max Health, nor can stacking inspect its implementation conflicts. The model receives a summary, not the previous output. Output quality itself was not sampled; omitted context is deterministic and forces users to re-supply implementation manually.
findings.evidence: changes.js:75-83 compactForApi sends only name/summary/modules/params/network notes and the first 2500 header characters; it drops cpp_source, pseudocode, graph and setup. Workspace.jsx:220 and :238 use it for regeneration and stacking. server.py:211-222 compacts again and :236 limits stacked headers to 1800 characters. :185-186 promises preserving unaffected content and integrating systems.
findings.expected: R-087: previous output is sent with explicit revision instructions; request: "regeneration should visibly respect the edits" and stack should "combine them into a single synthesized output ... avoids conflicts." Unchanged implementation and cross-system logic must be available to the model for a faithful revision/merge.
reproduction_steps: Open a saved system whose .cpp contains an implementation detail not in its header or summary.
Change only a parameter and Synthesize, or select it with another project and Stack.
Trace compactForApi and build_user_text: the complete source, pseudocode and graph are absent from the model input.
The model cannot faithfully revise/merge that omitted implementation.

findings.title: Phone users cannot reach generated output and tuning actions — desktop-only fixed panels exceed a viewport with hidden overflow

The header (:385-419) has unwrapped branding/actions. reproduction_steps: Open the signed-in workspace at 375px CSS width.
Generate a system and try to view the central tabs and tune the right panel.
Open a public share link at the same width and try its Copy JSON and tab actions.
Fixed rows exceed the clipped viewport with no responsive navigation.

findings.title: Assigning a tuning table does not initialize the generated component — export adds an uncalled helper instead of table-backed defaults
findings.surface: Plugin export Data Table and Setup Guide
findings.observed: Files, media and generated artifacts: for an ordinary system with tunables and no existing DataTable initialization, the exported component never reads the CSV/table. Designers must author extra Blueprint wiring instead of assigning a table, and the in-app Setup Guide omits this workaround. Numeric keys normalized by pascal (e.g. regen_rate -> RegenRate at :96) also only apply if a component property happens to have that exact name. Essential generation/export remains available, but the promised no-code tuning integration is missing.
findings.evidence: zipExport.js:176-177 writes the original header/source (only retargeting API on header); :178-183 separately adds tuning helper files and CSV. unrealExtras.js:127 defines ApplyTuningRow but :165-167 instructs users to manually add a BeginPlay call. No table property or read is injected into the component. Workspace.jsx:981 renders only result.setup_guide, not tuning.setup.
findings.expected: request: "The generated code reads its defaults from that table when one is assigned" and "The Setup guide gains steps for importing the table and assigning it"; R-304/R-305 require matching parameter names and actual component initialization with built-in fallback and Why notes.

Import the CSV in Unreal; assigning/creating a table alone cannot change this component's defaults without manually adding the helper call.

findings.title: Teammates cannot tell which invites failed after reopening — delivery results are never saved or rendered per invite

findings.observed: Messaging and notifications: inviting two people where one provider send fails and one succeeds yields transient toasts only. After reload the sender sees identical pending rows and cannot determine who needs the fallback link; links are also shown even for successful delivery. Both real send paths exist, but the persistent delivered/failed/not-attempted outcome is missing. Recovery requires manually contacting invitees.

TeamModal.jsx:77 and ShareModal.jsx:69 show only Joined/Invited; TeamModal.jsx:84 and ShareModal.jsx:71 show links without checking delivery.
findings.expected: R-288: "Each pending invite ... shows a delivery state of delivered, failed or not attempted ... and the same state appears after a page reload"; request: "On-screen links remain as a fallback when sending fails". Save and display each invitation's actual delivery result.
reproduction_steps: Invite one team/project member when the email provider rejects delivery.
Invite another when the provider accepts it.
Close/reopen the modal or reload; both rows show only Invited, and both have copyable links.

findings.title: Members with only team projects cannot start a bundle — action visibility counts Mine and Shared only
findings.surface: Projects > Team > selected projects
findings.observed: UI state, navigation and interaction: an invited teammate with zero personal/direct-shared projects and two team projects can tick both but has no Bundle as plugin button. Creating dummy personal projects or asking an owner for a preset is not the promised direct team workflow. Individual exports remain possible, so this is a bounded failure of multi-project export.

Team-readable projects must contribute to bundle action availability.

There is no Bundle as plugin action.

findings.title: Used and expired reset links still present a usable-looking form — reset page never validates tokens on entry
findings.surface: /reset/:token
findings.observed: UI state, navigation and interaction: recipients reopening a consumed or expired reset URL are invited to choose and enter a new password again, only to learn after submission that it cannot work. The backend prevents a second password change, but the refusal-on-open and recovery state are absent.
findings.evidence: AuthPages.jsx:45-50 initializes password/error only; :61-68 always renders the form regardless of token validity. Validation occurs only after submit (:54-58); backend/auth.py:286-288 correctly refuses used/expired tokens at that point.

Reload the same reset URL (or open one older than an hour).
The Choose a new password form is still rendered; refusal is delayed until another submit.

findings.title: Regenerating a system deletes its saved tests instead of marking them stale — synthesis replaces the entire system object
findings.surface: Tests tab after synthesis or Fix & regenerate
findings.observed: Data, persistence and APIs: starting with generated, saved tests, any successful synthesis (including the new structural-fix action) removes them from the workspace; pressing Save makes that loss current in storage. The Tests tab offers Generate instead of out-of-date tests. Developers must recover from old history or spend another request, rather than retain/review their test suite.
findings.evidence: Workspace.jsx:227 setResult({...data,...}) does not preserve result.tests. server.py:166-182 SystemOutput has no tests field, and :375/:383 serializes that model. TestsPanel.jsx:24 only computes stale when tests still exist; saveProject (:324-330) saves the replacement system.
findings.expected: R-297/R-298 and request: "A test file is kept with the project and marked 'out of date' when the system changes." Preserve the existing test source across regeneration, mark it stale, and replace it only on explicit test regeneration.
reproduction_steps: Generate tests and Save the project.
Change a system parameter and synthesize, or use Fix & regenerate.
Open Tests: the old source is gone rather than marked Out of date.
Save and reopen to persist the disappearance.

findings.title: Accepted test fixes vanish from notes and History — test acceptance bypasses fix recording
findings.surface: Tests > Accept fix; Save; Compare > History
findings.observed: Data, persistence and APIs: after accepting a test fix the user can save the repaired tests, but Save has no automatic fix note and History has no fix entry, review or selective Undo for it. reproduction_steps: Fix a Tests issue and Accept.
Press Save: no test-fix note is pre-filled.
Save and open History: that version has no entry for the accepted test fix.

findings.title: Malformed AI test replies can be accepted as generated tests or crash parsing — validation only looks for the substring It(
findings.surface: POST /api/ai/tests; Tests > Generate tests
findings.observed: AI and model features: a provider JSON reply whose code is prose containing It( passes the only code check and is shown as successful generated C++; a reply with cases:null raises TypeError outside the parser and becomes an unhandled 500 after consuming usage. Neither is a valid usable automation-test response. These are conditional source predictions, not observed model behavior.

reproduction_steps: Request Generate tests.
Consider a provider reply with code containing prose and the text It( but no automation definition: it is returned as successful test source.
Alternatively consider valid-looking code with cases:null: response construction raises instead of returning the controlled unreadable-tests error.

findings.title: Public-share plugin downloads omit COMPILE_REPORT.md — public exporter never supplies a report
findings.surface: Public share page > Unreal plugin .zip
findings.observed: Files, media and generated artifacts: recipients exporting a plugin from a supported public link get all plugin files but no compile report, regardless of known main/test issues. The workspace export supplies a report, but public recipients have no such alternative for that shared project without additional account access.
findings.evidence: PublicView.jsx:47 calls buildPluginZip(data.name,s,data.context) with only three arguments; zipExport.js:253 defaults report=null and :261 writes COMPILE_REPORT.md only if report is truthy.
findings.expected: R-306/request: "every zip (single plugin, source-only and bundle) includes COMPILE_REPORT.md"; checklist, Files, media and generated artifacts: trace all delivery consumers. Generate a report for public downloads as well.

Open it and press Unreal plugin .zip.
Inspect the source trace/zip construction: no COMPILE_REPORT.md is added.

findings.title: Exports claim no errors despite known test or bundle errors — warning, report and badge inputs omit whole issue sets
findings.surface: UE5 .zip export warning/README badge; bundle compatibility/report
findings.observed: Business logic and calculations: a project with clean main C++ but a missing AutomationTest.h test error exports without warning and gets a no-errors badge; bundles also omit those errors from reports. Additionally two individually clean systems with duplicate reflected class names show an explicit bundle conflict, yet the README can say no errors and COMPILE_REPORT omits it because shared conflicts never enter checks. Developers receive misleading compile status for a zip the app already knows has errors. No Unreal build was executed.
findings.evidence: Workspace.jsx:570 exportIssues comprises main activeIssues plus AI review only. :426-427 gates warnings on it and :440 passes it to badge calculation; :438 separately reports testIssues, proving known test errors exist. BundleModal.jsx:15-18 checks only checkSystem; :117 computes shared=bundleIssues(plan), but :124-125 sends only checks to report/buildBundleZip. zipExport.js:205/:326 grants a badge if those incomplete lists lack errors.

Bundle it with another project: the test error is absent from the bundle report.

Alternatively bundle two individually clean systems declaring the same class: UI shows a duplicate-class error, but README's aggregate badge and COMPILE_REPORT still use only the clean per-project lists.

findings.title: Known AI review errors disappear on reopen and in bundles — findings and model exist only in local React state
findings.surface: C++ AI review persistence; bundle reports and badge
findings.observed: Data, persistence and APIs: an AI-only compiler error is listed in C++ and the immediate single export, but Save/reopen, reload or opening a bundle loses it and its model. A module can then receive a clean badge and report None found without changing the faulty code. Developers and teammates lose the paid review's known result and get materially incomplete export status; rerunning reviews is the only user recovery.
findings.evidence: useAiReview stores results solely in React state (:43/:56) and clears them on system code/id changes (:45); review_cpp server.py:497 returns results without a project write; projects.detail(:65) returns system/context/ignores only. BundleModal activeIssues(:15-18) uses only checkSystem and :124 passes null for AI model.

Save and reopen the same project, or include it in a bundle.
The AI finding is absent; bundle's check/report uses only built-in issues and says no AI review ran.

findings.title: Compile reports omit the fix just exported — immediate export reads stale fix state and batch export never supplies fixes
findings.surface: Auto-fix Accept fix and export; download-only batch fix reports
findings.observed: Data, persistence and APIs: accepting the first auto-fix and exporting produces a report saying no fixes since last save despite exporting patched code. Download-only batch fixes also leave no fix record in their module's report. The artifacts themselves can contain correct fixed code, but reviewers lose the promised audit of how it changed.

Export and press Accept fix and export.
Read COMPILE_REPORT.md: the just-accepted change is absent.
Alternatively accept a batch fix for a view-only project and download: that unsaved fix is omitted too.

findings.title: Valid team names can turn email failures into 500s after committing invites — safety checks throw outside the failure handler
findings.surface: Team/project invites and forgot-password email failure handling
findings.observed: Third-party integrations: inviting to a valid team/project whose name includes 'CVV' (e.g. 'CVV Combat') raises an unhandled 500 after creating the invitation. The owner gets an error rather than the invite result/fallback guidance; retry updates its role without sending because the member already exists. The same unguarded validation can break the generic forgot-password response when an account's name includes a banned substring. This is source-predicted, not a provider observation.
findings.evidence: emailer.py:116 calls _assert_safe_email outside the try at :118. :72-74 raises ValueError on any listed substring, including 'cvv'. teams.py:131 commits the invite before :132 send_invite; team names flow into subject/body at :83-87. projects.py:417-419 similarly commits then sends.
findings.expected: R-265/R-287/request: "On-screen links remain as a fallback when sending fails" and invite remains pending/acceptable; checklist, Third-party integrations: failure must produce visible recoverable status. Treat safety-validation rejection as an email failure and still return the committed invite and emailed=false.
reproduction_steps: Create a team named CVV Combat.
Invite a valid teammate email.
The invite write precedes a ValueError during email validation, so the request fails instead of returning emailed=false.
Retry the invite: the existing-member branch changes its role and does not attempt delivery.

findings.title: Double-clicking batch Accept spends two requests on the next project — acceptance stays enabled during save and advances twice
findings.surface: Bundle > Fix all projects > Accept and save new version
findings.observed: UI state, navigation and interaction: double-clicking Accept and save new version while its PUT is pending starts two save/advance handlers. Optimistic versioning prevents the second write (409), but both handlers then start the next project's paid fix request, consuming two requests for one review. One competing result can replace the other, and the user sees a spurious save-conflict error. Main data is not double-saved, but quotas and review order are impaired.
findings.evidence: BundleModal.acceptBatchFix(:97-107) awaits the save without setting pending/consumed state; FixReviewModal:76 leaves Accept enabled. Each handler then calls advance(:115); :79 calls requestFix for the next project, which records usage/server.py:564 and sends a provider request/:566.
findings.expected: R-326/R-327: one accepted version and "one provider request ... once per request" per sequential review; checklist, UI state, navigation and interaction: "pending controls ... preserve one ... per intent." Consume/disable acceptance until save and advancement finish.
reproduction_steps: Start Fix all projects for at least two projects with issues.
In the first project's review, double-click Accept and save new version before the save completes.
Both handlers proceed to the next project and each sends a fix request; one earlier save gets a 409.

findings.title: Keyboard focus escapes review windows and Escape closes stacked dialogs — shared modal has no focus ownership or topmost handling
findings.surface: Shared Modal used by fix reviews, History, Team and Bundle
findings.observed: Layout, theme, visuals and UX: opening a fix, team or bundle modal does not move existing keyboard focus inside it; Tab can reach hidden workspace controls and Enter activate them. With History plus a fix detail open, Escape invokes both modal close handlers instead of only the active surface. Keyboard users lose review context and can initiate background work without seeing its control. This is source-predicted, not a measured accessibility run.
findings.evidence: Modal.jsx:5-9 attaches Escape on window for every mounted modal but has no focus transfer, trap, restoration, background inert state or scroll ownership. :11-12 overlays an aria-modal dialog only; HistoryModal remains mounted while FixDetailModal opens (Workspace.jsx:1179-1185).
findings.expected: checklist, Layout, theme, visuals and UX: "keyboard focus stays visible and follows the active surface" and dialogs restore focus; R-321/R-345 require usable review/modal controls. Prevent keyboard navigation into the obscured workspace and let only the top dialog handle Escape.
reproduction_steps: Focus a workspace control and open a team/fix/bundle modal.
Use Tab through controls: no focus boundary prevents returning to the workspace behind the dialog.
Open History then a fix detail and press Escape: both registered window listeners fire.

findings.title: Restoring old code keeps discarded fixes in pending History and reports — restore never clears fixLog or fixNotes
findings.surface: Compare > Restore version > History/Save/export
findings.observed: Data, persistence and APIs: restoring an older version after an unsaved accepted patch discards its code but leaves the patch in Not saved yet and auto-fill notes. The next save associates the discarded fix with the restored code, and exports report a fix no longer applied. The restored code itself is correct, but history/audit and selective undo are misleading.
findings.evidence: restoreVersion(:460-463) replaces project/system via openSystem but never clears fixLog/fixNotes. openSystem(:354-372) does not clear them either. saveProject(:330) submits fixLog for the next snapshot, and exportZip(:437) reports it as fixes since last save.
findings.expected: R-331/R-332: each version lists fixes "accepted before that save" for its actual code; request: restoring a version replaces unsaved fixes. checklist, Data, persistence and APIs: state changes propagate consistently to histories and reports.
reproduction_steps: Accept an unsaved fix on a saved project.
Restore an earlier version using Compare.
Open History: the discarded fix is still under Not saved yet.
Save or export: its fix entry/note/report accompanies code that no longer contains it.

findings.title: A late save erases the next project's unsaved fix history — completion guards metadata but clears global fix state unconditionally
findings.surface: Cross-project async Save completion and Fix History
findings.observed: Business logic and calculations: while A's slow save is pending, the user can open B and accept a fix. A's completion clears B's unsaved fix history/automatic note despite correctly leaving B's project metadata alone. The B code remains patched, but its accepted-change record is irrecoverably missing from the next version unless the user reconstructs it. Saving remains disabled during A's request, but Fix controls are not.
findings.evidence: saveProject(:333-337) guards setProject by savingFor, but :339-342 unconditionally closes the current save dialog and clears saveNote/fixNotes/fixLog even after a project switch. openProject(:380-381) starts the next project's independent fix queues; its new entries can then be cleared by this earlier response.
findings.expected: request (inherited fix): "Save ... results can no longer land on a project you switched to"; checklist, Business logic and calculations: "stale work must respect later decisions"; R-313/R-331 require accepted fixes/notes to remain until their own save.
reproduction_steps: Save project A while its network response is delayed.
Open B and accept a fix before A's save returns.
When A's save succeeds, B's fixLog and fixNotes are emptied.
Save B: its patch has no corresponding history entry or automatic note.

findings.title: Test-fix review can promise header repairs that Accept silently drops — test acceptance applies only the returned .cpp
findings.surface: Tests > Fix > before/after review > Accept fix
findings.observed: AI and model features: if the model proposes a header-only repair or a paired header/test change, the user sees and accepts both diffs, yet the header remains unchanged. For instance a proposed visibility correction allowing a test to call a component method is never applied, so that test still cannot compile despite the accepted review. This is conditional on the model response and was not executed.
findings.evidence: FixReviewModal.jsx:71-72 displays both data.cpp_header and data.cpp_source for test fixes. Workspace.jsx:1175 supplies the current header for that review, but :646 Accept only copies data.cpp_source into tests.code and silently ignores data.cpp_header. The normal code branch :657 copies both.
findings.expected: R-294/request: tests "can be fixed the same way" through the before/after review; checklist, UI state, navigation and interaction: material actions must apply exactly the reviewed approved changes. Enforce header read-only at the endpoint/review boundary, or apply a supported header edit explicitly and track it.
reproduction_steps: Request a Tests fix whose provider response changes the header as well as the tests (the endpoint accepts either file).
Review the displayed header/source changes and press Accept fix.
Only the tests source is installed; the approved header edit is discarded with no error.

findings.title: Growing team collections silently hide work and can revoke valid access — capped membership lists are reused for authorization
findings.surface: Team switcher, team project authorization/listing and Bundle presets list
findings.observed: Data, persistence and APIs: a user belonging to 101 teams loses the newest team from the switcher and loses project access through it because authorization reuses only the oldest 100 memberships. Similarly older presets and excess team projects silently disappear without paging. This is a growth-boundary prediction, not measured workload behavior; the demonstrated main harm is inaccessible listed work/membership, recoverable through reducing collections or direct-sharing projects but not through a next-page control.
findings.evidence: teams.my_teams(:35) sorts oldest first and to_list(100), then project_roles_via_team(:41) authorizes projects using only that truncated set. projects.py:187 caps team project rows at 1000 and :295/:306 cap preset lists at 200. No continuation cursor/count is returned and ProjectsPanel.jsx:28-29 builds the switcher only from the returned teams.
findings.expected: R-263: GET teams returns "exactly the teams the caller belongs to"; R-337: users may belong to several teams; checklist, Data, persistence and APIs: "pagination reaches the last page ... exposes truncation." Authorization must not use a truncated listing as the complete membership set.
reproduction_steps: Create or join more than 100 teams; create a project in the newest team.
Reload Projects > Team: that team is omitted from the oldest-first result.
A non-owner whose only access is that team gets Project not found on the project's GET because the role map excludes it.
For presets/team projects, exceed their result caps: no next page or truncation notice is available.

findings.title: Small fixes to long files can stall the review window — full-file quadratic diff runs before context filtering
findings.surface: Before/after fix review and Compare diff for long imported C++
findings.observed: Performance and resource leaks: importing a valid long .cpp with 20,000 short lines (within 60k chars) then reviewing a tiny fix builds about 400 million two-byte cells (~800 MB, plus row objects) and performs 400 million iterations synchronously on the UI thread. Filtering to nearby changed lines happens afterward and saves no work. This predicts serious browser unresponsiveness/memory pressure exactly when users must approve/discard, not an observed latency measurement.
findings.evidence: sideBySideDiff(:49) allocates (n+1) Uint16Arrays of (m+1) entries and :50-53 fills every cell. FixReviewModal:10 computes the whole diff before limiting display context at :11-18. server.py:512-513 allows up to 40k/60k characters, and projects.py:108 accepts imported system dictionaries without line bounds.
findings.expected: checklist, Performance and resource leaks: bound transformations and tie work growth to supported payloads; request: before/after review must remain usable for accepted source. Compute bounded hunks or otherwise avoid quadratic full-file allocation for a small patch.
reproduction_steps: Import a C++ system with a source containing roughly 20,000 short lines within the supported 60k-character fix bound.
Request and receive a small patch.
Open its review: FileDiff computes the entire 20,000 by 20,000 LCS matrix before rendering a few changed lines.

findings.title: Closing auto-fix review downloads a zip instead of canceling — modal Close is wired to Discard and export
findings.surface: Auto-fix-before-export review/error > X, Escape or backdrop
findings.observed: UI state, navigation and interaction: closing an auto-fix review or error with X, Escape or the backdrop downloads the unpatched zip immediately, even though the user did not choose either export action or Export without fixing. They can delete the unwanted download and restart, but cancellation does not work as the dialog affordance promises.
findings.evidence: FixReviewModal.jsx:44 supplies onDiscard as Modal.onClose; Modal.jsx:6/:11/:15 calls onClose on Escape/backdrop/X. Workspace.jsx:1177 invokes exportZip(thenExport,true) whenever that handler runs for a non-running auto-fix review/error.
findings.expected: R-317: "no zip downloads before one of [Accept fix and export or Discard and export] is pressed"; request: auto-fix must "Show the before/after review first"; checklist, UI state, navigation and interaction: cancel/close must respect the user's interruption instead of completing an unrelated action.
reproduction_steps: Enable Auto-fix before export and choose a plugin export with issues.
Wait for the fix review or error.

findings.title: Blueprint calls in renamed bundle modules point to the wrong class package — clipboard export ignores the resolved unique module name
findings.surface: Bundle plugin > second module's Blueprints/*_EventGraph.txt

The C++ modules themselves are still exported; this is a bounded Blueprint artifact failure, predicted from source without Unreal execution.

findings.title: Structural fixes cannot reliably preserve long custom code — regeneration silently truncates the previous system before the model call
findings.surface: Compile check > Fix & regenerate for long/imported systems
findings.observed: AI and model features: a supported imported project with custom declarations beyond header character 8,000 or implementation beyond source character 12,000 loses that code from the structural-fix model's input even though the client supplied it. The returned full replacement is not merged with the original. Developers cannot rely on unrelated custom behavior surviving this operation; reviewing/recovering it requires manual comparison or restoring a saved version. This establishes omitted grounding, not an observation that a particular model actually deleted a particular function.
findings.evidence: Workspace.jsx:273 sends result as previous_system for Fix & regenerate. build_user_text(server.py:275) calls compact_system(req.previous_system,8000,full=True). compact_system(:251/:254) slices the header at 8,000 characters and source at 12,000, while synthesis replaces the workspace system (Workspace.jsx:227); no merge restores the omitted suffix afterward.

Give the regenerating model the complete authoritative code or use a preservation mechanism for parts omitted from its context.

Trace the provider text: the unrelated suffix is absent.
The resulting full system replaces the original without restoring omitted regions.

findings.title: Ignored issues still interrupt exports — export fallback uses the unfiltered check results

Choose UE5 .zip > Unreal plugin.
The source predicts Check before export lists the ignored issues again.

findings.title: Developers cannot switch to a lighter model from the fix quota warning — Fix uses a two-choice browser confirm

findings.title: Viewers can invoke AI fixes despite the project role restriction — fix-cpp checks sign-in only

In contrast projects.py:233 enforces editor for ignores and :199 enforces editor for Save. Workspace.jsx:862 only hides Fix controls via canEdit={!readOnly}.

findings.title: Accepted fixes have no Discard changes recovery — workspace never offers the promised local revert

Decide not to keep the accepted patch, without saving.
Look for Discard changes: the workspace has no such action; Discard existed only before acceptance.

findings.title: Preset downloads can omit teammates' newer saves — Download uses the snapshot fetched when the dialog opened

Without closing the first dialog, Download the plugin.
The bundle builder receives the older system snapshot, without the new method.

findings.title: Preset users cannot identify which shared projects were skipped — inaccessible projects collapse into an anonymous count

ProjectsPanel.jsx:115 opens directly from the unfiltered list row.

Have their owner revoke access to the two shared projects.
Reopen the preset.
The skipped banner reports only the number, without names or ids; the specified item GET has no handler.

findings.title: A no-op AI patch is presented as an acceptable fix — edits are counted without checking whether code changed
findings.surface: POST /api/ai/fix-cpp; Review the fix modal
findings.observed: AI and model features: conditionally on a model returning an edit with identical find/replace text, the endpoint reports 200 with a change instead of no_changes. The developer sees a change list and Accept fix but no before/after diff, and accepting fixes nothing. findings.title: Rapid Ignore actions can be lost after reopening — whole-list writes are sent concurrently without ordering
findings.surface: C++ tab > Ignore / Restore; PUT /api/projects/{id}/ignores
findings.observed: Data, persistence and APIs: starting with [], Ignore A sends [A], then Ignore B sends [A,B]. If the second write commits before the first, the server ends with [A] while the screen shows both ignored. Reopening brings B back; independent teammate updates can likewise overwrite each other. This is a source-backed interleaving, not a measured race. Users can re-ignore, but cannot rely on their acknowledged choices surviving.
findings.evidence: Workspace.jsx:562 updates local ignores immediately, :563 fires api.put without awaiting/serializing it, and :565 sends the whole accumulated array. projects.py:235 unconditionally $sets the entire ignored_issues field, with no version predicate.
findings.expected: R-240/R-242: ignores are stored with the project and remain ignored after reopening; checklist, Data, persistence and APIs: 'Walk plausible interleavings ... [check] lost/overwritten valid work'. Each distinct acknowledged Ignore should survive its own earlier request finishing late.
reproduction_steps: On a project with two built-in issues, click Ignore on A then B before A's save completes.
Let the [A,B] request commit first, followed by the delayed [A] request.
Reopen the project: B is active again despite its prior Ignore confirmation.

findings.title: Changing the end of a long offending line does not revoke its ignore — issue identity truncates the source text
findings.surface: C++ compile check > Ignore; subsequent saved/regenerated code
findings.observed: Business logic and calculations: for a missing Engine/World.h warning on a source line over 300 characters, ignore it, then change an expression near the end of that same line without fixing the include. The message and first 300 key characters remain identical, so the changed line is still suppressed for the developer and teammates. This defeats the promised automatic expiry; recovery requires noticing and manually restoring the issue. The exact condition is equal truncated prefixes with different full line text.
findings.evidence: compileCheck.js:184 reads the trimmed source line, then :185 slices the complete file|message|text identity to 300 characters. Workspace.jsx:545-549 suppresses any issue whose truncated key matches a stored key; projects.py:125 likewise caps the stored key at 300.
findings.expected: request/R-243: 'An ignore stops applying if that issue's line text changes.' Identity must include all meaningful source text (for example a hash), not just a prefix; two different line texts must invalidate the old ignore.
reproduction_steps: Open/import code with GetWorld()-> usage and no Engine/World.h on a line longer than 300 characters.
Ignore that built-in warning and save the project.
Regenerate or import a revised system preserving the line's first 300 characters but changing its ending expression.
The warning's truncated key still matches and it stays ignored.

findings.title: Valid methods after nested helper types are reported as undefined — class lookup ignores closing scopes
findings.surface: C++ tab compile check and Fix these issue input
findings.observed: Business logic and calculations: in a UHealthComponent containing a plain nested FCache struct followed by UFUNCTION void Heal(), with UHealthComponent::Heal defined in the source, classAt returns FCache. The check reports 'UFUNCTION FCache::Heal ... never defined' and supplies this false issue to one-click Fix/export warnings. Developers must investigate/ignore the false diagnostic or risk approving an unnecessary AI repair. This is a deterministic source prediction, not an Unreal compile observation.
findings.evidence: compileCheck.js:110 records every class/struct opening, :111 returns the last opening preceding a UFUNCTION without tracking its closing brace, and :112 looks up that type's qualified definition. :130 emits a linker error when that mistaken qualified name is absent.
findings.expected: request: compile check links issues to 'the code that caused them'; checklist, Business logic and calculations: rules must use the correct object's identity. A method belongs to its enclosing class scope, not the nearest earlier type declaration, and an already defined valid method must not be labelled missing.
reproduction_steps: Import/open a header with UHealthComponent, a nested plain struct FCache { int Value; }; and then UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable) void Heal();.
Include a corresponding UHealthComponent::Heal() definition in the source.
Open C++: the new classAt logic searches for FCache::Heal instead and emits a false missing-definition error.

findings.title: Keyboard focus escapes fix and bundle dialogs — the shared modal never isolates or focuses its active surface
findings.surface: Review the fix / Writing a fix / Bundle preset dialogs
findings.observed: Layout, theme, visuals and UX: after keyboard activation of Fix these or opening a preset, focus remains in the workspace and Tab can reach underlying buttons instead of staying in the dialog. Keyboard users can unknowingly open another project or invoke background actions during review; closing does not reliably return focus to the trigger. Pointer backdrop protection does not prevent keyboard interaction. No browser focus sequence was executed; the absence of enforcement is established in the shared primitive.
findings.evidence: Modal.jsx:5-9 only registers Escape; :11-18 adds a backdrop and aria-modal but no initial focus, focus trap, inert background or focus restoration. FixReviewModal.jsx:42 uses that primitive, passing null onClose while running. The trigger remains mounted behind the dialog.

The new review must allow keyboard users to reach Accept/Discard without interacting with the hidden workspace.
reproduction_steps: Use the keyboard to activate Fix these or a Bundle presets row.
Press Tab repeatedly while the dialog is open.
The code provides no focus move/trap, so background controls remain in the tab order and can be activated behind the overlay.

findings.title: Older saved presets become inaccessible after 200 — the list silently truncates with no next page
findings.surface: Projects > Bundle presets list; GET /api/bundle-presets

Reload the Projects panel.

findings.title: Presets forget selected projects that are not ready yet — Save stores only currently exportable ids
findings.surface: Bundle into one plugin > Save as preset
findings.observed: Data, persistence and APIs: select Health, Stamina and Inventory where Inventory is readable but has no C++ yet. Because two valid modules remain, Save as preset succeeds but stores only Health/Stamina. When Inventory later acquires saved C++, reopening the preset still omits it forever; the user's chosen bundle intent was lost. They can recreate the preset manually, so this is recoverable.

The no-C++ system is merely described as skipped at :26, with no indication that saving a preset permanently drops its selection.

Open Bundle and Save as preset.
Later save C++ into the third project and reopen the preset.

findings.title: New stacked projects inherit another project's ignores — detaching the project leaves shared ignore state behind
findings.surface: Stack systems > new unsaved system > C++ check > Save project
findings.observed: Data, persistence and APIs: after ignoring a CoreMinimal.h warning in project A whose first line is #pragma once, stack two systems into a new unsaved system. If the generated header has that same warning/first line, it is already hidden by A's key; Save then persists A's ignore into the new project. Other teammates see a suppressed warning they never chose for this system. This is conditional on a matching diagnostic key in the new system, not an observed generation result.
findings.evidence: Workspace.jsx:290 detaches a successfully stacked system with setProject(null), but never clears ignores. :545-548 still filters the new system against the preceding project's keys. On the next new-project save, :329 writes the retained ignores to the newly created project. setIgnores is otherwise called only on openProject (:370) and ignore actions (:562).
findings.expected: R-240: ignored keys are 'scoped to that project'; request: ignores are 'saved with the project'. A new stacked project must not inherit unrelated projects' warning decisions without an explicit choice.
reproduction_steps: In saved project A ignore 'CoreMinimal.h is not included.' on first line #pragma once.
Use Stack on two projects and obtain a new header with that same first line/missing-include warning.
Open C++ on the new unsaved stacked system; the old ignore remains active.
Save it as a new project: the old key is copied into its ignored_issues.

findings.title: Reviewing a small fix can exhaust browser resources on high-line-count files — unchanged files still run a quadratic full diff
findings.surface: Review the fix modal for accepted high-line-count .cpp input
findings.observed: Performance and resource leaks: a supported 60,000-character source containing 20,000 short '//\n' comment lines plus short code can approach 20,000 lines. Even a header-only fix computes the unchanged source's full ~400 million-cell LCS matrix: roughly 800 MB of typed-array storage plus overhead, synchronously in React render. This predicts severe browser resource pressure/unresponsiveness during review for that bounded input, not measured latency or a claim that typical projects freeze. Discard is not usable until rendering completes.
findings.evidence: FileDiff in FixReviewModal.jsx:8-9 calls sideBySideDiff before its equality return at :19, including for an unchanged .cpp. changes.js:49 allocates (n+1) Uint16Array(m+1) rows and :50-53 visits every cell. FixRequest accepts cpp_source up to 60000 characters (server.py:512).
findings.expected: checklist, Performance and resource leaks: 'Estimate work/resource growth ... material responsiveness ... loss'; the promised review must remain usable for accepted files, especially when only the other file changed.
reproduction_steps: Import a valid source near 60,000 characters with about 20,000 short comment/blank lines and a header with one repairable issue.
Run a fix that changes only the header, leaving cpp_source byte-identical.
When the reply arrives, FileDiff still allocates and computes the quadratic source diff before discovering that it is unchanged.

Unreal's own include contract is explicit in the code: a header containing HealthAndDamageComponent.generated.h must be saved as HealthAndDamageComponent.h, not a human display title.

The title-based filenames do not match the includes; compare with the canonical names used by Source files only zip export.

findings.title: Saved presets appear to disappear during a transient load failure — errors are converted into an empty hidden list
findings.surface: Projects > Bundle presets list on initial load or refresh failure

The code clears the list and removes its heading instead of showing failure and a retry action.

findings.title: AI review can report a malformed answer as clean — invalid issue entries are silently discarded
findings.surface: POST /api/ai/review-cpp; C++ Snippets → AI review
findings.observed: AI and model features: when the provider returns a list containing malformed issue records, the endpoint converts an unreadable review into a successful empty review. A developer is incorrectly reassured the review found no additional problems and can export without those warnings. Actual provider output was not executed; this is the exact source-predicted consequence for those responses. Retrying the review is possible but the UI gives no reason to do so.

Thus {"issues":["missing implementation"]} or {"issues":[{"file":".cpp"}]} becomes {issues:[]}. frontend/src/components/CompileCheck.jsx:80 displays "No further problems found." for that response; Workspace.jsx:571 also receives no AI export warnings.

Consider a provider response whose JSON issues array contains a string issue, or an object missing message.

The panel displays No further problems found and export has no AI issue warning.

findings.title: Plugin exports using WidgetLayoutLibrary fail to build without edits — dependency detection omits its UMG module
findings.surface: UE5 .zip → Unreal plugin; Bundle plugin → Download
findings.observed: Files, media and generated artifacts: a valid stored system that includes Blueprint/WidgetLayoutLibrary.h and calls UWidgetLayoutLibrary::GetViewportScale, with no other UMG-matching symbols, exports with only Core/CoreUObject/Engine dependencies. WidgetLayoutLibrary belongs to UMG, so this otherwise valid UI system cannot compile/link as the advertised drop-in plugin until a developer edits Build.cs. The same failure affects a selected bundle module. This is a source prediction; Unreal compilation was not run.

findings.title: A restored version can lose its provenance note during a concurrent save — backfill wins the snapshot race and restore swallows the duplicate
findings.surface: Compare → Restore vN; concurrent project Save; Version history

Restore's v3 insert then hits the unique index and is silently ignored. Before restore inserts the v3 snapshot, have a second editor load v3 and save it as v4.
The second save backfills v3 without a note.

findings.title: AI review and synthesis fail when usage accounting cannot write — counter insertion is a mandatory unhandled prerequisite
findings.surface: C++ Snippets → AI review; Synthesize; daily usage accounting

Under a failed llm_usage insert (for example a write failure on that collection), press AI review or Synthesize.

No model request is actually sent, despite the accounting being ancillary.

findings.title: A delayed save conflict offers to overwrite the wrong project — only successful replies check the captured project identity
findings.surface: Save → delayed conflict response → switch project → Newer version saved

Press Save on A, then dismiss the Save dialog while its request is delayed.
Open project B from Projects before A's 409 arrives.
Observe the predicted Newer version saved dialog naming A's saver over B; Load their version reloads B and Overwrite with mine forcibly saves B.

R-212 promises a disabled running review followed by its result, not a fresh idle review while the same operation remains active.

The newly mounted panel has an enabled AI review button; press it to start another request.

findings.title: Developers cannot AI-review code with more than 40 local issues — client sends an array the endpoint rejects

findings.title: Near-limit users can synthesize without any quota warning — cached client usage is never rechecked before the server starts work

findings.observed: Business logic and calculations: leave tab B open after it fetched a low count, then consume 450 of the key's 500 estimated requests in tab A. Tab B still sees its old low count and starts a new synthesis without warning or confirmation; the server also never checks authoritative usage. The same bypass occurs while the initial usage fetch is pending. Users lose the promised advance notice and can unexpectedly spend their remaining quota. Source predicts this stale-tab lifecycle; no provider quota was consumed in review. Reloading first is possible but undiscoverable because B displays an apparently current daily count.

findings.title: Acknowledged saves can lose their notes or history entries — snapshot writes race after the project commit and failures are ignored
findings.surface: Save with version note; Restore version; Compare → History
findings.observed: Data, persistence and APIs: a successful save can permanently lose its version note. After A commits v2 but before its snapshot insert, B can read v2, backfill it with an empty note, and advance to v3; A's unique-key failure is silently swallowed. Users cannot repair the missing note through the label-only UI; existing current system data remains available. These are source-backed interleavings, not runtime observations.
findings.evidence: projects.py:191-195 commits the project update before :203 inserts its snapshot; :185-189 lets a concurrent saver backfill the new current version using snapshot(project) with the default empty note. :204-205 swallows all snapshot insert exceptions. findings.expected: R-191: saves "write [the note] onto the snapshot they create"; R-177: restore "creates a new newest version" and "leaves every earlier version intact"; checklist, Data, persistence and APIs: "Multi-document operations leave no half-written state on failure." Preserve the submitted note and snapshot alongside every acknowledged version.

Before A's snapshot insert, editor B reads v2 and saves v3; B's pre-save backfill creates the v2 snapshot with no note.
